title: Introduction
preview: This chapter translates the business framing and technical choices established in the previous chapters into a structured design baseline for . Its purpose is to identify what the platform must do, which constraints it must respect, who will interact with it, and how the final multi-layer architecture answers those needs. Unlike Chapter 3, which focused on tool selection, this chapter focuses on requirement formaliza
preview2: tion and on the architectural organization of the implemented solution. In practice, the design logic follows the same principles emphasized in modern data-intensive system engineering: clear separation of concerns, explicit data movement boundaries, and layered coordination between storage, compute, and access services .

title: Requirement Elicitation Context
preview: The requirements of were derived from three complementary sources: the business objective of creating a distributed customer-data foundation under the broader vision; the engineering need to ingest, store, process, validate, orchestrate, expose, and monitor heterogeneous customer-related datasets; the operational reality of a lightweight academic multi-node environment with security hardening requirements. As a resul
preview2: t, the chapter does not present abstract requirements in isolation. Each requirement is directly connected to an implemented capability of the platform and to the final distributed deployment model.

preview: At the logical level, is organized as a layered customer-data platform rather than as a monolithic data pipeline. title: Security-by-Design Integration
preview: Security is not positioned as an external afterthought. It is integrated into the design of the platform through explicit controls attached to core layers. This follows the same engineering rationale as the rest of the architecture: identity, traffic protection, and protected storage boundaries are treated as part of the system design itself, not as a late operational patch . title: Design Rationale and Trade-offs
preview: The final design is the result of deliberate engineering trade-offs rather than maximum-complexity choices: the architecture demonstrates real service distribution while remaining feasible on lightweight academic VMs. the system is decomposed into clear responsibilities to strengthen maintainability and defense clarity. the security layer reinforces the platform without changing its lakehouse logic. explicit scripts,
preview2: bundles, checks, and service roles make the deployment easier to explain and debug. the design prepares downstream Customer 360 and AI use cases without pretending that those intelligent modules are already fully implemented. These trade-offs are important for the jury defense because they show that the architecture was shaped by real constraints, not by arbitrary tool accumulation.
